newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Cosmonauts reported safe after fire on Mir.
newsitem.headline: Cosmonauts reported safe after fire on Mir.

text.p: Six cosmonauts, including an American and a German, were forced to don gas masks when fire broke out on the ageing Russian space station Mir but officials said on Monday they were in no danger.

The seven-minute blaze in an air filtering unit on Sunday night released fumes that irritated the crew's throats. It was the latest in a series of mishaps to bedevil the 12-year-old station, which is the world's only permanent orbiting craft.

It came hours before Russian space officials announced money troubles had forced a delay in the launch of the first module of its replacement, the international space station Alpha, casting new doubts over Moscow's ability to participate in the project.
An officer with Russia's military space forces said the Mir blaze was "not a serious incident".
"There was no need to evacuate the Mir crew," he said.
Mission control officials said, however, that the crew were still wearing masks on Monday as they continued to test the air in the craft. Mir has already outlasted its expected lifespan.
U.S. astronaut Jerry Linenger, a doctor, had given his fellow crewmen a clean bill of health, officials said.
Film released by mission control showed some crew members wearing full-face rubber gas-masks, while others had on masks covering only their nose and mouth.

A crew member filmed the site of the blaze, allowing ground control experts to assess the damage. It was hard to judge the scale of the damage from the film released to the media but some metal components were melted and twisted out of shape.

Yuri Koptev, head of the Russian Space Agency, said on Monday the first Alpha module would be launched in June next year, rather than this November. The delay this would cause to the international project was Russia's fault.
"The timetable will be changed because of Russia, which did not build a service module on time," he said.
The new space station, to be complete by 2003, is being funded by Russia, the United States, the European Space Agency, Canada, Italy and Japan.
Russia is building the first module, a cargo section, and the third, a service area where cosmonauts will live and work.

Some U.S. officials already say Moscow, which also blames cash shortages for long delays in building the third module, is not pulling its weight. A delay in launching the first module will also delay launch of the second stage, a docking module being built in the United States. After the third module, other parts of the station will be attached in stages by 2003.

"The problem is with the service module, which if not finished on time will unravel the whole project," James Sensenbrenner, chairman of the U.S. House of Representatives' Science Committee, said last week.
Alpha will cost a total of $37 billion and will replace Russia's ageing Mir orbiting station,
Sunday's blaze highlighted the problems facing the Russian space complex, once the jewel of the Soviet industrial crown, but which has suffered years of underfunding and wage delays.

"Forty two percent of our top specialists have left the space industry in the last five years," Koptev said. "Only 14 space enterprises have paid wages without delay. We owe the federal budget 220 billion roubles ($40 million)."
State financing for space was just one seventh of that in Soviet days, but cooperation with foreign firms was now offering domestic companies a lifeline worth millions of dollars.
